    11	/-!
    12	# The translated rank-one cover brick
    13	
    14	This file records the part of the separably-closed cover argument that is already consumable by
    15	the landed fibre API.  A `BaseFieldTranslationDrop` keeps the input class `lambda` in the
    16	presentation equation, chooses its base-field translating class explicitly, and records the
    17	positive-twist/point-subtraction output.  The consumer below turns that output into the exact
    18	`IsSplitWitness` shape used by `chartLocus`.
    19	
    20	The arbitrary-affine family of `PicRankOneLocalPresentation` objects required by
    21	`PicRankOneOpen` is deliberately not inferred from `h0 = 1` and `H1 = 0`: no such producer is
    22	landed in the current API.  The final theorem therefore exposes the field-level consumer and
    23	keeps that family producer as an explicit integration obligation.
    24	-/
    25	
    26	set_option autoImplicit false
    27	set_option maxSynthPendingDepth 3
    28	
    29	universe u
    30	
    31	open CategoryTheory Limits MonoidalCategory CartesianMonoidalCategory
    32	open TopologicalSpace Opposite
    33	
    34	namespace AlgebraicGeometry
    35	
    36	open AlgebraicJacobian
    37	
    38	attribute [local instance] Scheme.overModule Scheme.overSectionsAlgebra
    39	attribute [local instance 10000] relCurve.instOver
    40	
    41	variable {k : Type u} [Field k] {C : Over (Spec (.of k))}
    42	variable [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom] [IsProper C.hom]
    43	  [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom]
    44	
    45	noncomputable section
    46	
    47	/-! ## The positive-twist input -/
    48	
    49	section PositiveTwist
    50	
    51	variable {K : Type u} [Field K] {Y : Scheme.{u}} [IsIntegral Y]
    52	  [Y.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
    53	  [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 (Y ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
    54	  [LocallyOfFiniteType (Y ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
    55	  [QuasiCompact (Y ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
    56	  [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (Y.moduleKSheaf K) 0)]
    57	  [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (Y.moduleKSheaf K) 1)]
    58	
    59	/-- The FLV class theorem in the spelling used by the translated-cover lane.
    60	
    61	The class `l` is the presenting class of the input fibre, while `theta` is the positive
    62	base-field twist.  Keeping this as a named wrapper makes the positive-twist step visible at the
    63	call site; it does not manufacture a presentation or hide the input class in an unrelated
    64	existential. -/
    65	theorem exists_positive_twist_vanishing
    66	    (π : Y ⟶ P1 K) [IsFinite π] [IsDominant π]
    67	    (hπ : π ≫ P1.structureMap K = Y ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))
    68	    (l θ : Y.CechPic) (hθ : 1 ≤ classDeg K θ) :
    69	    ∃ n₀ : ℕ, ∀ n ≥ n₀, ∀ W : Y.CurveDivisor,
    70	      Scheme.CurveDivisor.picClass K W = l * θ ^ n →
    71	        Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (Y.divisorSheaf K W) 1) := by
    72	  exact exists_subsingleton_hModule_one_of_one_le_classDeg_of_isFinite_toP1
    73	    π hπ l θ hθ
    74	
    75	end PositiveTwist
    76	
    77	/-! ## The lambda-tied drop package -/
    78	
    79	section DropPackage
    80	
    81	variable {K L : Type u} [Field K] [Algebra k K]
    82	  [Field L] [Algebra k L] [Algebra K L] [IsScalarTower k K L]
    83	  [Module.Finite K L] [Algebra.IsSeparable K L]
    84	
    85	/-- Data for the positive twist and the subsequent point subtraction.
    86	
    87	`hM₀` ties the splitting field presentation to the particular input `mu`; `hW₀` says that the
    88	divisor being reduced is in the positive twist class (the chart index is zero at this stage).
    89	`baseSubtraction` is intentionally an explicit class-level bridge: it says that the divisor
    90	returned by the greedy reduction is represented by a base-field divisor.  The current tree has
    91	the graph-class version of this bridge but no divisor pullback operation, so this hypothesis is
    92	kept visible rather than replaced by a fieldwise existential. -/
    93	structure SepClosedTranslatedDropData (μ : picEt C (overSpec k K)) where
    94	  m : ℕ
    95	  M₀ : (relCurve C L).CechPic
    96	  hM₀ : PicEtAff.map C L (picEtAffineEquiv C K μ) =
    97	    PicEtAff.unit C L (relPicMk C (overSpec k L) M₀)
    98	  W₀ : ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left).CurveDivisor
    99	  hW₀ : Scheme.CurveDivisor.picClass L W₀ =
   100	    M₀ * Scheme.CechPic.map (relCurveMap C k L)
   101	      (chartTwistClass C m (0 : (C ⊗ overSpec k k).left.CurveDivisor))
   102	  genusValue : ℕ
   103	  excess : ℕ
   104	  hχ : Sheaf.chi (C.left.moduleKSheaf k) = 1 - (genusValue : ℤ)
   105	  hdeg : Scheme.CurveDivisor.deg L W₀ = (genusValue : ℤ) + excess
   106	  h1 : Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule
   107	    ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left.divisorSheaf L W₀) 1)
   108	  P : Set ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left)
   109	  hdense : ∀ U : ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left).Opens,
   110	    (U : Set ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left)).Nonempty → (P ∩ U).Nonempty
   111	  hPcl : ∀ x ∈ P, x ≠ genericPoint ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left)
   112	  hPdeg : ∀ x ∈ P, ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left).residueDeg L x = 1
   113	  baseSubtraction : ∀ (S : ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left).CurveDivisor),
   114	    0 ≤ S → Scheme.CurveDivisor.deg L S = (excess : ℤ) →
   115	      (∀ (x : (C ⊗ overSpec k L).left) (hx : x ≠ genericPoint _),
   116	        coeffAt hx S ≠ 0 → x ∈ P) →
   117	      ∃ Z : (C ⊗ overSpec k k).left.CurveDivisor,
   118	        Scheme.CurveDivisor.picClass L S =
   119	          Scheme.CechPic.map (relCurveMap C k L)
   120	            ((chartTwistClass C 0 Z)⁻¹)
   121	
   122	/-- The output of the positive-twist/drop construction, tied to both the input class and the
   123	base-field translating divisor.
   124	
   125	The final field is the existing fibre consumer.  In particular, `S` is not merely a divisor
   126	with the right cohomology: `baseClass` identifies its class with the base change of `Z`, and
   127	`translated` is about `mu` translated by the resulting base-field class
   128	`chartTwistClass C d.m Z`. -/
   129	structure SepClosedTranslatedDropResult (μ : picEt C (overSpec k K))
   130	    (d : SepClosedTranslatedDropData (C := C) (L := L) μ) where
   131	  S : ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left).CurveDivisor
   132	  Z : (C ⊗ overSpec k k).left.CurveDivisor
   133	  nonnegative : 0 ≤ S
   134	  degree : Scheme.CurveDivisor.deg L S = (d.excess : ℤ)
   135	  support : ∀ (x : (C ⊗ overSpec k L).left) (hx : x ≠ genericPoint _),
   136	    coeffAt hx S ≠ 0 → x ∈ d.P
   137	  baseClass : Scheme.CurveDivisor.picClass L S =
   138	    Scheme.CechPic.map (relCurveMap C k L) ((chartTwistClass C 0 Z)⁻¹)
   139	  h0_one : Sheaf.h0
   140	    ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left.divisorSheaf L (d.W₀ - S)) = 1
   141	  h1_vanishing : Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule
   142	    ((C ⊗ overSpec k L).left.divisorSheaf L (d.W₀ - S)) 1)
   143	  translated : IsSplitWitness C
   144	    (μ * thetaFamily C (chartTwistClass C d.m Z) (overSpec k K))
   145	
   146	/-- Positive twisting followed by point subtraction produces the exact field-level translated
   147	rank-one witness.
   148	
   149	The greedy theorem supplies `S`, `h0 = 1`, and preservation of `H1 = 0`.  The explicit
   150	`baseSubtraction` bridge then supplies the base divisor `Z`; class arithmetic shows that
   151	`W₀ - S` presents `mu` translated by the base-field class `chartTwistClass C d.m Z`.  The last
   152	line applies the existing `IsSplitWitness` consumer, so no unrelated Picard class can satisfy
   153	the conclusion. -/
   154	theorem exists_sepClosedTranslatedDropResult
   155	    (μ : picEt C (overSpec k K))
   156	    (d : SepClosedTranslatedDropData (C := C) (L := L) μ) :
   157	    Nonempty (SepClosedTranslatedDropResult (C := C) (L := L) μ d) := by
   158	  obtain ⟨-, S, hS0, hSdeg, hSsupport, hS0one, hS1⟩ :=
   159	    exists_isSplitWitness_of_drop C μ d.m
   160	      (0 : (C ⊗ overSpec k k).left.CurveDivisor)
   161	      d.genusValue d.excess d.hχ d.M₀ d.hM₀ d.W₀ d.hW₀ d.hdeg d.h1
   162	      d.P d.hdense d.hPcl d.hPdeg
   163	  obtain ⟨Z, hSZ⟩ := d.baseSubtraction S hS0 hSdeg hSsupport
   164	  have hW : Scheme.CurveDivisor.picClass L (d.W₀ - S) =
   165	      d.M₀ * Scheme.CechPic.map (relCurveMap C k L)
   166	        (chartTwistClass C d.m Z) := by
   167	    have hW₀ := d.hW₀
   168	    unfold relCurveMap relCurve at hW₀ hSZ ⊢
   169	    rw [sub_eq_add_neg, Scheme.CurveDivisor.picClass_add, Scheme.picClass_neg,
   170	      hW₀, hSZ]
   171	    simp only [map_inv, inv_inv]
   172	    rw [mul_assoc, ← map_mul]
   173	    simp only [chartTwistClass, Scheme.CurveDivisor.picClass_zero, inv_one, mul_one,
   174	      pow_zero, one_mul]
   175	  have htranslated : IsSplitWitness C
   176	      (μ * thetaFamily C (chartTwistClass C d.m Z) (overSpec k K)) :=
   177	    isSplitWitness_of_witness_twistClass C μ d.m Z d.M₀ d.hM₀
   178	      (d.W₀ - S) hW hS1
   179	  exact ⟨{
   180	    S := S
   181	    Z := Z
   182	    nonnegative := hS0
   183	    degree := hSdeg
   184	    support := hSsupport
   185	    baseClass := hSZ
   186	    h0_one := hS0one
   187	    h1_vanishing := hS1
   188	    translated := htranslated
   189	  }⟩
   190	
   191	end DropPackage
   192	
   193	end
   194	
   195	end AlgebraicGeometry

name: horizon
description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
---

You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.

## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate

Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.

You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
**shared state**, not meetings:

- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
  another team.
- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).

Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
object in `horizon inbox list --json`.

## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)

**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.

The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):

- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
  item's status/strategy current as you work. It doubles as the **project board**:
  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but
  leave their closure to the human unless asked otherwise (skill: `horizon-inbox`).
- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See
  "Pace yourself" below for how to act on it.

## Your session's identity (environment variables)

The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |

## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)

Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:

- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).

## One-shot discipline (important)

This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).

## Pick the highest-value work

Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.

If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
the objective is large. Leave a concise task comment only for a durable state
change or blocker, not every action. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
(it returns to the queue).

## Fresh-context checkpoints

The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
checkpoints:

- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
  clean/build result.

Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
terminal `done` claim.

Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.

## Warnings are work

Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
why.

Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
issue rather than repeated no-op calls.

## Do the work (Lean)

For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
configured final build covers the same files.

**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
mathlib — query it:

| You want | Use | Not |
|---|---|---|
| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |

`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
back to grep.

Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.

- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.

## Read the other projects

They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.

## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)

Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
needs no permission.

Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute

name: horizon-inbox
description: Read and act on the Archon Horizon inbox — list/filter items, understand labels/kinds, comment, archive, create; per-team ownership and read-state; and message other projects or teams via the `horizon inbox` CLI.
---

The inbox is the durable channel between the human, agent sessions (present and
future), and other projects. Act on it through the CLI; never edit inbox files
by hand. Prefer `--json` whenever reading command output for exact ids or
fields.

## Read

- `horizon inbox list` — read the inbox. Use `--json` when you need exact ids,
  labels, scope, author, audience, timestamps, or comments. Use the list filters
  to narrow without losing the overview: `--to horizon`, `--to human`,
  `--project P`, repeated `--kind K`, repeated `--label L`,
  `--status open`, `--query TEXT`, `--limit N`, and `--comments N`.
- In an agent session, an unqualified list means the **open working queue**, not
  archived history. It is ordered by attention: required protections first,
  unread/direct conversations next, then advisory items. JSON starts with an
  `attention` summary so redirecting stderr cannot erase this signal.
- `horizon inbox show <id> --json` opens exactly one item and marks it read for
  your team. Use `--no-mark-read` for inspection without acknowledgement.
- Every inbox command evaluates the full local working set, even when `list` is
  filtered. Treat its advisory warnings as a prompt to review duplicates, stale
  memories, and consumed notices. The CLI never archives automatically because
  only the working agent can decide what is resolved; that agent must make an
  explicit cleanup pass before its final report.
- Labels are the release gate. Local inbox items default to `agent-ready`, which
  means they are visible to agents at run boundaries. Keep that default for
  machine-addressed work, and usually keep it for human-addressed notices too:
  it helps later agents see that the human has already been notified and avoids
  duplicate reports. Use `not-ready`, `rejected`, or no labels only when there is
  a concrete reason agents should not see or act on the item yet.
- Audience says who should read the item: empty/general, `horizon`, `human`,
  `project:<name>`, or a **direct message** to another team: `task:<id>` /
  `run:<id>` (older items may carry the legacy `ground` audience). A conversation
  may have several recipients; start one with `horizon inbox dm <recipient>...`.
  Scope/project says what the item is about.
- Horizon reads general items, items addressed to `horizon`, items addressed
  to its project, and DMs addressed to its own task/run. It should ignore other
  projects' and other teams' addressed items.
- A conversation's participants are its recipients **and its initiator**. The
  initiator is recorded as `metadata.started_by`; replies become unread for every
  other participant, including that initiator. Participants are not ownership:
  the initiator remains responsible for deciding when the thread is finished.
- Kinds: `conversation` (a direct/group thread requiring prompt acknowledgement),
  `hint` (normal guidance), `issue` (problem to fix/report),
  `protection` (standing constraint / soft freeze), `info` (a notice for the
  human — something you did or noticed they should know, e.g. a renamed project
  or an important change; purely informational, never affects what runs),
  `memory` (durable agent note or dead end).

## Ownership & read-state (your team's inbox)

Each running session is a **team**, and the inbox is shared across teams. Two
lightweight overlays keep it navigable:

- **Ownership** — an item is either *shared with everyone* (the default) or
  *owned by one task* (that team's private inbox — e.g. its own memory). Read your
  team's inbox with `horizon inbox list --mine` (owned-by-you **plus** shared);
  another team's private items don't appear. Own an item to your task with
  `horizon inbox add --mine …` (or `--owner <task-id>`), and `horizon inbox own
  <id> --mine|--owner <task>|--shared` to move an existing one. Owning your
  `--kind memory` notes keeps another team's memory out of your working set.
- **Read-state** — read/unread is **per team**, so a shared item several teams see
  tracks who has read it. `horizon inbox list --unread` is what *you* have not read
  yet; `horizon inbox read <id>` marks it read, and `horizon inbox unread <id>`
  puts it back (e.g. you read it but it still needs action). Combine:
  `horizon inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue — the same signal
  the pre-command synchronizer counts for you.

Read in this order before editing:

1. `horizon inbox list --mine --status open --kind protection --json` — every
   active protection is required even if your team previously marked it read.
2. `horizon inbox list --mine --unread --kind conversation --json` — open each
   result with `inbox show`; reply when a response is needed, otherwise the read
   acknowledgement clears it until another participant replies.
3. Consult hint/issue/info/memory items as advisory context for the task.

The reader/owner id is inferred from your session (your task), so you rarely pass
it explicitly.

## Act

Authorship is automatic: every item and comment you create through the CLI is
attributed to your role (normally `horizon`) from the run environment — you do
**not** pass `--author` (a stray `--author work-reviewer` is demoted to the
`agent` metadata, not used as the author, so the author set stays conventional).
If you are a dispatched **subagent**, add `--agent <your-name>` (e.g. `--agent
work-reviewer`) to record your identity; it is stored in metadata and shown
next to the role in the UI, keeping the author itself a clean role. Items and
comments are also auto-tagged with the run/session provenance (a small chip in the
UI); you do not pass this yourself.

New inbox items use a two-part body:

- First paragraph = concise title. Keep it short enough to scan in one UI row
  (aim for under ~100 characters); do not put the full explanation here.
- Second paragraph and later = non-empty description. Put the evidence, impact,
  next action, and relevant ids/files here. The description is **mandatory** — an
  item that is only a title is rejected.

Write bodies and comments in **Markdown**: the dashboard renders it. Operational
messages are deltas, not reports. Default to one sentence or at most three short
bullets covering conclusion, new evidence, and next action; do not repeat the
thread, commit diff, or session history. Use headings only when a genuinely
multi-part decision needs them. Agent comments target at most 600 characters and
are rejected above 1200; descriptions/opening messages target 800 and are
rejected above 2400. Humans are not subject to these bounds.

Do not create an item whose body is only a title. If you need a `[persistent]` or
`[temporary]` tag, put it at the start of the title paragraph and keep the rest
of that paragraph concise.

Before opening a new item, search the open inbox for the same topic using
`horizon inbox list --status open --query "key words" --json` and, when relevant,
`--project P` / `--to R`. If a live item already covers the same issue, do not
open a duplicate: add a comment with the new evidence, or edit the body if the
main description is stale. If you discover an open item is obsolete, already
solved, consumed, or superseded, add a short comment when the reason is not
obvious and then run `horizon inbox archive <id>`.

### Conversation lifecycle

A conversation is for an expected reply, decision, or active coordination. A
one-way handoff or announcement is an `info`/`hint`, not a conversation.

1. **Search before starting:** inspect open conversations for the same topic and
   participants (`inbox list --status open --kind conversation --query "key words"
   --json`). Reply to the existing thread whenever it can carry the update. Do not
   open one thread per incremental finding.
2. **One question, one thread:** keep follow-ups, answers, corrections, and the
   final decision as comments on that thread. Start another only when it has a
   genuinely different decision boundary or participant set.
3. **Answer before branching:** when a conversation becomes unread, open it and
   answer or acknowledge it before starting another conversation with the same
   team.
4. **The initiator closes:** if `metadata.started_by` is your task/run, you own
   the lifecycle. Once the requested answer has arrived and been consumed, add a
   short conclusion comment when the outcome is not obvious, then
   `horizon inbox archive <id>`. Do this during the session, not only after a
   warning says the inbox is full.
5. **Do not hide an answer from its initiator:** recipients normally reply and
   leave closure to the initiator. For a human-started thread, answer it but leave
   it open for the human to consume/archive unless the human explicitly delegates
   closure. Use `complete` instead of `archive` only when the concluded thread is
   intentionally meant to remain visible in the resolved working record.
6. **End-of-session sweep:** before the final report, inspect open conversations
   in which your task is `started_by`. Archive every resolved one and state a real
   blocker on any that must remain open. An accumulation of open conversations is
   unfinished coordination, not harmless history.

- `horizon inbox comment <id> --body "..."` — progress note on an item (record
  what changed; not to ask the human for clarification). Do not write your name
  into the body; authorship is automatic. Comment only at a **key advance** such
  as a milestone, ruled-out route, blocker, correction, or conclusion. Update the
  existing thread with the delta instead of re-establishing its full context.
- `horizon inbox dm task:<id> [task:<id> ...] --body "Topic\n\nOpening message"`
  — start a one-to-one or group conversation. Use `horizon ps` to discover live
  teams. Use it only after the lifecycle search above. The sender remains a
  participant and owns closure; every reply makes the thread unread for the other
  participants. Humans read and reply from the live dashboard.
- **Write comments as mathematics, for a human.** State the key step that
  succeeded in human-readable mathematical language (LaTeX for formulas), naming
  the result and the idea — e.g. "Proved $H^i(X,\mathcal{F})=0$ for $i>\dim X$ by
  reducing to the affine case via Čech cohomology." Mention Lean declaration
  names and file paths only as supporting detail; the substance is the maths, not
  a code changelog. This applies to comments on **roadmap items and tasks** too:
  when a key step lands, record it there in the same mathematical, legible style.
- `horizon inbox archive <id>` — soft-delete: keep the item for the record but
  hide it from the dashboard by default. Use for stale, superseded, consumed, or
  no-longer-key context. Keeping the inbox tidy this way is your job (or the
  janitor subagent's) — prune memory/info so they remain small.
  For a conversation you initiated, this is the normal "discussion finished"
  operation after its answer/conclusion has been consumed.
- `horizon inbox complete <id>` — mark an item resolved only when it records work
  you genuinely concluded and want to keep visible outside the archive. Before
  completing, add a short **conclusion comment**: first the mathematical
  conclusion (what was proved/established, in words + LaTeX), then concise
  metadata (runs, approximate LOC, files/declarations involved). A reader should
  grasp the result and how it was concluded without opening the logs.
- `horizon inbox add --body "Short title\n\nDescription with details and next action." [--to R] [--project P] [--persistent|--temporary] [--agent <name> if a subagent]`
  — open a new item.
  - `--to` is the recipient: `horizon`, `human`, `project:<name>`, or a direct
    message to another team `task:<id>` / `run:<id>`.
    Use `--to project:<name>` to message another project (e.g. "I rewrote your
    `foo` declaration more cleanly, you may want it"); use `--to task:<id>` to
    message a specific running team.
  - `--owner <task-id>` / `--mine` keeps the item in one team's inbox instead of
    the shared default.
  - `--project` says what the item is ABOUT (its subject).
  - `--persistent` / `--temporary` just prepend a `[persistent]` / `[temporary]`
    tag to the body.
  - `--pending` labels the item `not-ready` instead of the default `agent-ready`,
    so it stays invisible to agents until a human releases it.
- `horizon inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body "Short memory title\n\nDurable fact, convention, or dead end."` — record a durable
  note / dead end. Memory lives in the inbox, so it is rendered in the "Memory"
  section and a human can prune it like any other item.
- `horizon inbox protect --body "..." [--project P] [--file F] [--declaration D] [--blueprint-node N]`
  — add a semantic standing constraint the Horizon agent must respect (a soft freeze),
  e.g. "do not change the signature of `Foo.bar`". These render as a
  "Protected" section; honour them, including semantic ones. For a target that
  must be mechanically blocked before dispatch, the user uses the config-backed
  `horizon freeze add <file|declaration|blueprint-node> <target>` command instead.

Reading convention: an item tagged `[persistent]` is a standing rule — respect
it every round and keep it open while relevant. `[temporary]` (or untagged) is
one-shot — archive it once consumed. Items in the "Protected" section are never
modified.

    10	
    11	/-!
    12	# Chart-module structure of the m-chart glued sheaf (DAT-1, stage 1c)
    13	
    14	The `Γ(X, V)`-module and coefficient-ring properties of the glued section module
    15	`F(V)` on an affine chart `V` carrying a finite subordinate trivializing basic-open
    16	family (`informal/spec-dat-1.md`, decision (D5)): sections `h : ι → Γ(X, V)` whose
    17	basic opens `D(h i)` lie in gluing pieces (`hP : D(h i) ≤ U (σ i)`) and span the unit
    18	ideal (`hspan : Ideal.span (Set.range h) = ⊤` — the worksheet partition witness feeds
    19	this through `Ideal.span_range_eq_top_of_sum_eq_one`).
    20	
    21	All statements are relative to an ambient packaging
    22	`[Scheme.QcohOn (gluedSheaf k U g) V]` whose action is componentwise (the hypothesis
    23	`hq`, discharged by `rfl` for packagings built by `gluedQcohOn` — the same interface as
    24	`gluedPairData`), with the chart module structure `Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE` bound by
    25	`letI` in statements (RE-0 pattern) and the section modules in the sheaf-object
    26	spelling `(gluedSheaf k U g).obj.obj (op W)` — the spelling the engine consumes.
    27	
    28	* `gluedPieceModule`/`gluedPieceEquiv` — each piece `F(D(h i))` is a free rank-one
    29	  `Γ(X, D(h i))`-module through the piece trivialization `gluedTriv`;
    30	* `isUnit_algebraMap_end_glued` — a chart section restricting to a unit acts invertibly
    31	  on the glued sections of an open below a piece (trivialization conjugation);
    32	* `isLocalizedModule_secResₗ_glued` — **the RE-0 bridge fired per piece**:
    33	  `F(V) → F(D(h i))` is an `IsLocalizedModule (Submonoid.powers (h i))` (the abstract
    34	  bridge at `V ⊓ D(h i)`, transported across the opens equality `V ⊓ D(h i) = D(h i)`
    35	  by `IsLocalizedModule.of_linearEquiv`);
    36	* the localization-local chart properties: `moduleFinite_glued`,
    37	  `finitePresentation_glued`, `flat_glued`, `projective_glued` (over `Γ(X, V)`), and
    38	  the coefficient-ring transports `flat_glued_of_flat` (under `Module.Flat k Γ(X, V)` —
    39	  a benign weakening of the spec's freeness hypothesis: free ⟹ flat) and
    40	  `projective_glued_of_free` (under `Module.Free k Γ(X, V)`);
    41	* `moduleFinite_aeval'_glued` — the `AEval'`-finiteness export: an endomorphism acting
    42	  as the packaged action of a chart coordinate `a₀` has `k[X]`-finite chart lattice
    43	  whenever `Scheme.mulSectionEnd k a₀` does (the landed E-i input), through
    44	  `RigidEngine.moduleFinite_aeval'_of_smul_finite` and `moduleFinite_glued`.
    45	-/

    47	set_option autoImplicit false
    48	
    49	universe u
    50	
    51	open CategoryTheory Limits Opposite TopologicalSpace Polynomial
    52	
    53	/-! ## A partition of unity spans the unit ideal -/
    54	
    55	/-- **Span-⊤ from a partition of unity**: if `∑ i, a i * h i = 1` in a commutative ring,
    56	the range of `h` generates the unit ideal. -/
    57	theorem Ideal.span_range_eq_top_of_sum_eq_one {A : Type u} [CommRing A] {ι : Type*}
    58	    [Fintype ι] (a h : ι → A) (hpart : ∑ i, a i * h i = 1) :
    59	    Ideal.span (Set.range h) = ⊤ := by
    60	  rw [Ideal.eq_top_iff_one, ← hpart]
    61	  exact Ideal.sum_mem _ fun i _ =>
    62	    Ideal.mul_mem_left _ _ (Ideal.subset_span (Set.mem_range_self i))
    63	
    64	namespace AlgebraicGeometry
    65	
    66	section Module
    67	
    68	variable (k : Type u) [CommRing k] {X : Scheme.{u}} [X.Over (Spec (.of k))]
    69	
    70	attribute [local instance] Scheme.overModule
    71	
    72	variable {J : Type u} (U : J → X.Opens) (g : ∀ i j : J, Γ(X, U i ⊓ U j)ˣ)
    73	
    74	/-! ## Restriction bookkeeping -/
    75	
    76	/-- Componentwise restriction composes. -/
    77	lemma gluedRes_gluedRes {W'' W' W : X.Opens} (h₁ : W'' ≤ W') (h₂ : W' ≤ W)
    78	    (s : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W)) :
    79	    gluedRes k U g h₁ (gluedRes k U g h₂ s) = gluedRes k U g (h₁.trans h₂) s :=
    80	  Subtype.ext (funext fun _ => by
    81	    simp only [gluedRes_coe, Scheme.resHom_resHom])
    82	
    83	/-- Componentwise restriction along `W ≤ W` is the identity. -/
    84	lemma gluedRes_self {W : X.Opens} (hW : W ≤ W) (s : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W)) :
    85	    gluedRes k U g hW s = s :=
    86	  Subtype.ext (funext fun _ => Scheme.resHom_self _ _)
    87	
    88	/-! ## The coefficient action of a structure-morphism scalar -/
    89	
    90	/-- The componentwise action of the image `X.overAlgebraMap k V c` of a coefficient
    91	`c : k` agrees with the `k`-module action on glued sections. -/
    92	lemma gluedQsmul_overAlgebraMap {V W : X.Opens} (hWV : W ≤ V) (c : k)
    93	    (m : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W)) :
    94	    gluedQsmul k U g hWV (X.overAlgebraMap k V c) m = c • m := by
    95	  refine Subtype.ext (funext fun j => ?_)
    96	  have hc : (c • m).val j = c • m.val j := rfl
    97	  rw [gluedQsmul_coe, hc, Scheme.overModule_smul_def]
    98	  congr 1
    99	  exact X.overAlgebraMap_apply_res k (homOfLE (inf_le_left.trans hWV)).op c
   100	
   101	variable {V : X.Opens} {ι : Type u} {σ : ι → J} {h : ι → Γ(X, V)}
   102	
   103	/-! ## The piece module structure -/
   104	
   105	/-- **The `Aᵢ := Γ(X, D(h i))`-module structure on a piece** `Mᵢ := F(D(h i))`,
   106	transported through the `k`-linear piece trivialization `tᵢ : Mᵢ ≃ₗ[k] Γ(X, D(h i))`:
   107	`a • m := tᵢ⁻¹ (a * tᵢ m)`. This makes `Mᵢ` free of rank one over `Aᵢ`
   108	(`gluedPieceEquiv`). -/
   109	@[reducible] noncomputable def gluedPieceModule (hc : Scheme.IsGluingCocycle U g)
   110	    (hP : ∀ i : ι, X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ U (σ i)) (i : ι) :
   111	    Module Γ(X, X.basicOpen (h i)) ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g (X.basicOpen (h i))) where
   112	  smul a m := (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (a * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m)
   113	  one_smul m := by
   114	    change (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (1 * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m) = m
   115	    rw [one_mul, LinearEquiv.symm_apply_apply]
   116	  mul_smul a b m := by
   117	    change (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (a * b * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m) =
   118	      (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm
   119	        (a * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)
   120	          ((gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (b * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m)))
   121	    rw [LinearEquiv.apply_symm_apply, mul_assoc]
   122	  smul_zero a := by
   123	    change (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (a * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) 0) = 0
   124	    rw [map_zero, mul_zero, map_zero]
   125	  smul_add a m n := by
   126	    change (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (a * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) (m + n)) =
   127	      (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (a * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m) +
   128	        (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (a * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) n)
   129	    rw [map_add, mul_add, map_add]
   130	  add_smul a b m := by
   131	    change (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm ((a + b) * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m) =
   132	      (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (a * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m) +
   133	        (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (b * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m)
   134	    rw [add_mul, map_add]
   135	  zero_smul m := by
   136	    change (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (0 * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m) = 0
   137	    rw [zero_mul, map_zero]
   138	
   139	lemma gluedPieceModule_smul_def (hc : Scheme.IsGluingCocycle U g)
   140	    (hP : ∀ i : ι, X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ U (σ i)) (i : ι)
   141	    (a : Γ(X, X.basicOpen (h i))) (m : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g (X.basicOpen (h i)))) :
   142	    letI := gluedPieceModule k U g hc hP i
   143	    a • m = (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (a * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m) :=
   144	  rfl
   145	
   146	/-- **Each piece is `Aᵢ`-free of rank one**: the piece trivialization `tᵢ`, promoted to
   147	an `Aᵢ`-linear equivalence `Mᵢ ≃ₗ[Aᵢ] Aᵢ` for the `gluedPieceModule` structure. -/
   148	noncomputable def gluedPieceEquiv (hc : Scheme.IsGluingCocycle U g)
   149	    (hP : ∀ i : ι, X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ U (σ i)) (i : ι) :
   150	    letI := gluedPieceModule k U g hc hP i
   151	    ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g (X.basicOpen (h i))) ≃ₗ[Γ(X, X.basicOpen (h i))]
   152	      Γ(X, X.basicOpen (h i)) :=
   153	  letI := gluedPieceModule k U g hc hP i
   154	  { toFun := gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)
   155	    map_add' := (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).map_add
   156	    map_smul' := fun a m => by
   157	      change gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)
   158	          ((gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm (a * gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m)) =
   159	        a • gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m
   160	      rw [LinearEquiv.apply_symm_apply, smul_eq_mul]
   161	    invFun := (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm
   162	    left_inv := (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).left_inv
   163	    right_inv := (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).right_inv }
   164	
   165	@[simp]
   166	lemma gluedPieceEquiv_apply (hc : Scheme.IsGluingCocycle U g)
   167	    (hP : ∀ i : ι, X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ U (σ i)) (i : ι)
   168	    (m : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g (X.basicOpen (h i)))) :
   169	    gluedPieceEquiv k U g hc hP i m = gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i) m :=
   170	  rfl
   171	
   172	@[simp]
   173	lemma gluedPieceEquiv_symm_apply (hc : Scheme.IsGluingCocycle U g)
   174	    (hP : ∀ i : ι, X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ U (σ i)) (i : ι)
   175	    (t : Γ(X, X.basicOpen (h i))) :
   176	    (gluedPieceEquiv k U g hc hP i).symm t = (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).symm t :=
   177	  rfl
   178	
   179	/-- **The piece `Aᵢ`-action restricted along `A → Aᵢ` is the chart action**: for
   180	`r : Γ(X, V)`, the `Aᵢ`-scalar `X.resHom … r` acts on `Mᵢ` as the componentwise chart
   181	action `gluedQsmul`. -/
   182	lemma gluedPieceModule_smul_resHom (hc : Scheme.IsGluingCocycle U g)
   183	    (hP : ∀ i : ι, X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ U (σ i)) (i : ι) (r : Γ(X, V))
   184	    (m : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g (X.basicOpen (h i)))) :
   185	    letI := gluedPieceModule k U g hc hP i
   186	    (X.resHom (X.basicOpen_le (h i)) r) • m =
   187	      gluedQsmul k U g (X.basicOpen_le (h i)) r m := by
   188	  letI := gluedPieceModule k U g hc hP i
   189	  apply (gluedTriv k hc (σ i) (hP i)).injective
   190	  rw [gluedTriv_gluedQsmul k U g hc, gluedPieceModule_smul_def,
   191	    LinearEquiv.apply_symm_apply]

   193	/-! ## The packaged chart module structure: scalar towers and the RE-0 bridge -/
   194	
   195	section Packaged
   196	
   197	variable [Scheme.QcohOn (gluedSheaf k U g) V]
   198	
   199	/-- `IsScalarTower k Γ(X, V) F(W)` for any `W ≤ V`: the coefficient action of the
   200	packaging factors through the structure map `k → Γ(X, V)`. -/
   201	lemma isScalarTower_coeff
   202	    (hq : ∀ {W : X.Opens} (hW : W ≤ V) (r : Γ(X, V)) (s : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W)),
   203	      Scheme.QcohOn.qsmul (F := gluedSheaf k U g) hW r s = gluedQsmul k U g hW r s)
   204	    {W : X.Opens} (hWV : W ≤ V) :
   205	    letI : Module Γ(X, V) ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W) :=
   206	      Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g) hWV
   207	    letI : Algebra k Γ(X, V) := (X.overAlgebraMap k V).toAlgebra
   208	    IsScalarTower k Γ(X, V) ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W) := by
   209	  letI : Module Γ(X, V) ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W) :=
   210	    Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g) hWV
   211	  letI : Algebra k Γ(X, V) := (X.overAlgebraMap k V).toAlgebra
   212	  refine IsScalarTower.of_algebraMap_smul fun c m => ?_
   213	  change Scheme.QcohOn.qsmul (F := gluedSheaf k U g) hWV (X.overAlgebraMap k V c) m
   214	    = c • m
   215	  rw [hq hWV (X.overAlgebraMap k V c) m]
   216	  exact gluedQsmul_overAlgebraMap k U g hWV c m
   217	
   218	/-- `IsScalarTower Γ(X, V) Γ(X, D(h i)) Mᵢ`: the packaged chart action factors through
   219	the restriction `Γ(X, V) → Γ(X, D(h i))` and the piece module structure. -/
   220	lemma isScalarTower_chart_piece (hc : Scheme.IsGluingCocycle U g)
   221	    (hq : ∀ {W : X.Opens} (hW : W ≤ V) (r : Γ(X, V)) (s : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W)),
   222	      Scheme.QcohOn.qsmul (F := gluedSheaf k U g) hW r s = gluedQsmul k U g hW r s)
   223	    (hP : ∀ i : ι, X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ U (σ i)) (i : ι) :
   224	    letI := gluedPieceModule k U g hc hP i
   225	    letI : Module Γ(X, V) ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g (X.basicOpen (h i))) :=
   226	      Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g) (X.basicOpen_le (h i))
   227	    IsScalarTower Γ(X, V) Γ(X, X.basicOpen (h i))
   228	      ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g (X.basicOpen (h i))) := by
   229	  letI := gluedPieceModule k U g hc hP i
   230	  letI : Module Γ(X, V) ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g (X.basicOpen (h i))) :=
   231	    Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g) (X.basicOpen_le (h i))
   232	  refine IsScalarTower.of_algebraMap_smul fun r m => ?_
   233	  change (X.resHom (X.basicOpen_le (h i)) r) • m =
   234	    Scheme.QcohOn.qsmul (F := gluedSheaf k U g) (X.basicOpen_le (h i)) r m
   235	  rw [hq (X.basicOpen_le (h i)) r m]
   236	  exact gluedPieceModule_smul_resHom k U g hc hP i r m
   237	
   238	/-- **Invertibility of the packaged action of a unit**: a chart section `r` restricting
   239	to a unit on an open `W` below a gluing piece acts invertibly on `F(W)` — the action is
   240	conjugate, through the piece trivialization, to multiplication by the unit `r↾_W`. This
   241	discharges the `map_units` hypothesis of the RE-0 bridge. -/
   242	lemma isUnit_algebraMap_end_glued (hc : Scheme.IsGluingCocycle U g)
   243	    (hq : ∀ {W : X.Opens} (hW : W ≤ V) (r : Γ(X, V)) (s : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W)),
   244	      Scheme.QcohOn.qsmul (F := gluedSheaf k U g) hW r s = gluedQsmul k U g hW r s)
   245	    {W : X.Opens} (hWV : W ≤ V) {j : J} (hWj : W ≤ U j) (r : Γ(X, V))
   246	    (hr : IsUnit (X.resHom hWV r)) :
   247	    letI := Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g) hWV
   248	    IsUnit (algebraMap Γ(X, V)
   249	      (Module.End Γ(X, V) ((gluedSheaf k U g).obj.obj (op W))) r) := by
   250	  letI := Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g) hWV
   251	  have hE : ⇑(algebraMap Γ(X, V)
   252	      (Module.End Γ(X, V) ((gluedSheaf k U g).obj.obj (op W))) r) =
   253	      fun m : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W) => gluedQsmul k U g hWV r m := by
   254	    funext m
   255	    rw [Module.algebraMap_end_apply]
   256	    exact hq hWV r m
   257	  rw [Module.End.isUnit_iff, hE]
   258	  obtain ⟨v, hv⟩ := hr
   259	  refine Function.bijective_iff_has_inverse.mpr
   260	    ⟨fun m => (gluedTriv k hc j hWj).symm
   261	      ((↑v⁻¹ : Γ(X, W)) * gluedTriv k hc j hWj m), fun m => ?_, fun m => ?_⟩
   262	  · change (gluedTriv k hc j hWj).symm
   263	      ((↑v⁻¹ : Γ(X, W)) * gluedTriv k hc j hWj (gluedQsmul k U g hWV r m)) = m
   264	    rw [gluedTriv_gluedQsmul k U g hc hWV hWj r m, ← hv, Units.inv_mul_cancel_left,
   265	      LinearEquiv.symm_apply_apply]
   266	  · change gluedQsmul k U g hWV r
   267	      ((gluedTriv k hc j hWj).symm ((↑v⁻¹ : Γ(X, W)) * gluedTriv k hc j hWj m)) = m
   268	    apply (gluedTriv k hc j hWj).injective
   269	    rw [gluedTriv_gluedQsmul k U g hc hWV hWj, LinearEquiv.apply_symm_apply, ← hv,
   270	      Units.mul_inv_cancel_left]
   271	
   272	/-- **The RE-0 bridge fired on a piece** (DAT-1 (1c)): on an affine chart `V`, the
   273	restriction `F(V) → F(D(h i))` exhibits the piece sections as the localization of the
   274	chart sections at the powers of `h i`. The abstract bridge
   275	(`Scheme.QcohOn.isLocalizedModule_secResₗ`) produces this at `V ⊓ D(h i)` — its
   276	`map_units` hypothesis is the trivialization conjugation `isUnit_algebraMap_end_glued` —
   277	and `IsLocalizedModule.of_linearEquiv` transports across the opens equality
   278	`V ⊓ D(h i) = D(h i)`. -/
   279	theorem isLocalizedModule_secResₗ_glued (hV : IsAffineOpen V)
   280	    (hc : Scheme.IsGluingCocycle U g)
   281	    (hq : ∀ {W : X.Opens} (hW : W ≤ V) (r : Γ(X, V)) (s : ↥(gluedSubmodule k U g W)),
   282	      Scheme.QcohOn.qsmul (F := gluedSheaf k U g) hW r s = gluedQsmul k U g hW r s)
   283	    (hP : ∀ i : ι, X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ U (σ i)) (i : ι) :
   284	    letI := Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g) (le_refl V)
   285	    letI := Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g) (X.basicOpen_le (h i))
   286	    IsLocalizedModule (Submonoid.powers (h i))
   287	      (Scheme.QcohOn.secResₗ (F := gluedSheaf k U g)
   288	        (X.basicOpen_le (h i)) (le_refl V)) := by
   289	  letI := Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g) (le_refl V)
   290	  letI := Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g) (X.basicOpen_le (h i))
   291	  letI := Scheme.QcohOn.moduleOfLE (F := gluedSheaf k U g)
   292	    (inf_le_left : V ⊓ X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ V)
   293	  -- the unit-action hypothesis on `V ⊓ D(h i)`, an open below the piece `U (σ i)`
   294	  have hru : IsUnit (X.resHom (inf_le_left : V ⊓ X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ V) (h i)) := by
   295	    have h1 : IsUnit (X.resHom (X.basicOpen_le (h i)) (h i)) :=
   296	      X.toRingedSpace.isUnit_res_basicOpen (h i)
   297	    have h2 : X.resHom (inf_le_left : V ⊓ X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ V) (h i) =
   298	        X.resHom (inf_le_right : V ⊓ X.basicOpen (h i) ≤ X.basicOpen (h i))
   299	          (X.resHom (X.basicOpen_le (h i)) (h i)) := by
   300	      rw [Scheme.resHom_resHom]

     9	/-!
    10	# The pinned cocycle datum on the relative curve (DAT-1, stage 1d-i, the datum)
    11	
    12	The **cocycle datum over a `k`-algebra `B`** of the Wave-4 datum worksheet §3.2
    13	(BINDING; `informal/spec-dat-1.md` §0), on the pinned relative cover
    14	`relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)` of the relative curve `C_B`:
    15	
    16	* `AlgebraicGeometry.BasicOpenCoverData` — the two finite index types `J₀, J₁`, the
    17	  basic-open generators `h_j ∈ Γ(Vᵢᴮ, 𝒪)` and the partition witnesses
    18	  `∑ j, a_j · h_j = 1` per pinned chart; `pieces` sends `J₀ ⊕ J₁` to the basic opens
    19	  `D(h_j)`.
    20	* `AlgebraicGeometry.BasicOpenCocycleDatum` — the cover data together with the
    21	  transition units on the pairwise basic-open overlaps (`Units` bundle the inverse
    22	  witnesses) and the cocycle law `Scheme.IsGluingCocycle`.
    23	* `BasicOpenCocycleDatum.sheaf` — the glued sheaf of `B`-modules of the datum
    24	  (`gluedSheaf`), with the quasi-coherence packagings on **both pinned charts** and on
    25	  the **overlap** as instances (`instQcohOn₀/₁/Inf`, from `gluedQcohOn`: side-`i`'s own
    26	  family on chart `i`; side-0's family restricted along `V₀ᴮ ⊓ V₁ᴮ ≤ V₀ᴮ` on the
    27	  overlap, through the subordinate-pieces interface).
    28	* `BasicOpenCocycleDatum.pairData` — the two-cover pair data at the pinned relative
    29	  coordinates `t₀ᴮ, t₁ᴮ` (`relFiberCoord₀/₁`), through `gluedPairData` (the
    30	  componentwise-action hypotheses are `rfl` for the keyed instances).
    31	
    32	The engine keystones fired on `pairData.pair` are in
    33	`AlgebraicJacobian.Cohomology.GluedSheafEngine`.
    34	-/
    35	
    36	set_option autoImplicit false
    37	set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false
    38	
    39	universe u
    40	
    41	open CategoryTheory TopologicalSpace Opposite
    42	
    43	namespace AlgebraicGeometry
    44	
    45	attribute [local instance] Scheme.overModule
    46	
    47	variable {k : Type u} [Field k] (C : Over (Spec (.of k)))
    48	variable (B : Type u) [CommRing B] [Algebra k B]
    49	variable (π : C.left ⟶ P1 k)
    50	
    51	/-- **The basic-open cover data over `B`** (worksheet §3.2, first half): finite index
    52	types `J₀, J₁`, for `j ∈ Jᵢ` a section `h_j` of the pinned chart `Vᵢᴮ` with partition
    53	witnesses `∑ j, a_j · h_j = 1` in `Γ(Vᵢᴮ, 𝒪)` — so the basic opens `D(h_j)` cover the
    54	chart (`le_iSup_basicOpen_of_sum_eq_one`). -/
    55	structure BasicOpenCoverData [IsAffineHom π] : Type (u + 1) where
    56	  /-- The chart-0 index. -/
    57	  J₀ : Type u
    58	  /-- The chart-1 index. -/
    59	  J₁ : Type u
    60	  /-- The chart-0 index is finite. -/
    61	  fintype₀ : Fintype J₀
    62	  /-- The chart-1 index is finite. -/
    63	  fintype₁ : Fintype J₁
    64	  /-- The chart-0 basic-open generators. -/
    65	  h₀ : J₀ → Γ(relCurve C B, (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₀)
    66	  /-- The chart-1 basic-open generators. -/
    67	  h₁ : J₁ → Γ(relCurve C B, (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₁)
    68	  /-- The chart-0 partition coefficients. -/
    69	  a₀ : J₀ → Γ(relCurve C B, (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₀)
    70	  /-- The chart-1 partition coefficients. -/
    71	  a₁ : J₁ → Γ(relCurve C B, (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₁)
    72	  /-- The chart-0 partition witness. -/
    73	  partition₀ : ∑ j : J₀, a₀ j * h₀ j = 1
    74	  /-- The chart-1 partition witness. -/
    75	  partition₁ : ∑ j : J₁, a₁ j * h₁ j = 1
    76	
    77	attribute [instance] BasicOpenCoverData.fintype₀ BasicOpenCoverData.fintype₁
    78	
    79	namespace BasicOpenCoverData
    80	
    81	variable {C B π} [IsAffineHom π] (D : BasicOpenCoverData C B π)
    82	
    83	/-- The gluing index of the datum, `J = J₀ ⊕ J₁`. -/
    84	abbrev index : Type u := D.J₀ ⊕ D.J₁
    85	
    86	/-- The pieces of the datum: the basic opens `D(h_j)` of the two pinned charts. -/
    87	noncomputable def pieces : D.index → (relCurve C B).Opens :=
    88	  Sum.elim (fun j => (relCurve C B).basicOpen (D.h₀ j))
    89	    (fun j => (relCurve C B).basicOpen (D.h₁ j))
    90	
    91	@[simp]
    92	lemma pieces_inl (j : D.J₀) :
    93	    D.pieces (Sum.inl j) = (relCurve C B).basicOpen (D.h₀ j) := rfl
    94	
    95	@[simp]
    96	lemma pieces_inr (j : D.J₁) :
    97	    D.pieces (Sum.inr j) = (relCurve C B).basicOpen (D.h₁ j) := rfl
    98	
    99	/-- The chart-0 pieces cover the pinned chart `V₀ᴮ`. -/
   100	lemma cover₀ : (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₀ ≤
   101	    ⨆ j : D.J₀, (relCurve C B).basicOpen (D.h₀ j) :=
   102	  le_iSup_basicOpen_of_sum_eq_one D.a₀ D.h₀ D.partition₀
   103	
   104	/-- The chart-1 pieces cover the pinned chart `V₁ᴮ`. -/
   105	lemma cover₁ : (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₁ ≤
   106	    ⨆ j : D.J₁, (relCurve C B).basicOpen (D.h₁ j) :=
   107	  le_iSup_basicOpen_of_sum_eq_one D.a₁ D.h₁ D.partition₁
   108	
   109	/-- The chart-0 generators, restricted to the overlap of the pinned charts. -/
   110	noncomputable def hInf (j : D.J₀) :
   111	    Γ(relCurve C B,
   112	      (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₀ ⊓ (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₁) :=
   113	  (relCurve C B).resHom inf_le_left (D.h₀ j)
   114	
   115	/-- The restricted chart-0 pieces are subordinate to the pieces of the datum. -/
   116	lemma basicOpen_hInf_le (j : D.J₀) :
   117	    (relCurve C B).basicOpen (D.hInf j) ≤ D.pieces (Sum.inl j) := by
   118	  rw [hInf, Scheme.basicOpen_resHom, pieces_inl]
   119	  exact inf_le_right
   120	
   121	/-- The restricted chart-0 pieces cover the overlap of the pinned charts (the
   122	partition witness restricts to a partition witness). -/
   123	lemma coverInf : (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₀ ⊓ (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₁
   124	    ≤ ⨆ j : D.J₀, (relCurve C B).basicOpen (D.hInf j) := by
   125	  refine le_iSup_basicOpen_of_sum_eq_one
   126	    (fun j => (relCurve C B).resHom inf_le_left (D.a₀ j)) D.hInf ?_
   127	  have hres := congrArg
   128	    ((relCurve C B).resHom (inf_le_left : (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₀ ⊓
   129	      (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₁ ≤ (relCover C B (fiberTwoCover π)).V₀))
   130	    D.partition₀
   131	  rw [map_sum, map_one] at hres
   132	  rw [← hres]
   133	  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun j _ => (map_mul _ _ _).symm
   134	
   135	end BasicOpenCoverData
   136	
   137	/-- **The pinned cocycle datum over `B`** (worksheet §3.2, VERBATIM): the basic-open
   138	cover data of the two pinned charts together with transition units on the pairwise
   139	basic-open overlaps (with explicit inverse witnesses — `Units`) satisfying the cocycle
   140	identities in the overlap section rings (`Scheme.IsGluingCocycle`, including the
   141	normalization `g j j = 1`). This is the DAT-1 constructor input and the object RE-5
   142	descends. -/
   143	structure BasicOpenCocycleDatum [IsAffineHom π] : Type (u + 1) extends
   144	    BasicOpenCoverData C B π where
   145	  /-- The transition units on the pairwise piece overlaps. -/
   146	  unit : ∀ i j : toBasicOpenCoverData.index,
   147	    Γ(relCurve C B, toBasicOpenCoverData.pieces i ⊓ toBasicOpenCoverData.pieces j)ˣ
   148	  /-- The cocycle law. -/
   149	  isGluingCocycle : Scheme.IsGluingCocycle toBasicOpenCoverData.pieces unit
   150	
   151	namespace BasicOpenCocycleDatum
   152	
   153	variable {C B π} [IsAffineHom π] (D : BasicOpenCocycleDatum C B π)
   154	
   155	/-- **The glued sheaf of the datum**: the m-chart cocycle-glued sheaf of `B`-modules on
   156	the small Zariski site of the relative curve `C_B`. -/
   157	@[reducible] noncomputable def sheaf :
   158	    Sheaf (Opens.grothendieckTopology ((relCurve C B : Scheme.{u}) : TopCat))
   159	      (ModuleCat.{u} B) :=
   160	  gluedSheaf B D.pieces D.unit
   161

     9	/-!
    10	# Meromorphic presentations of Čech Picard classes
    11	
    12	On an integral scheme `X`, every nonempty open contains the generic point `η`, and
    13	sections embed into the function field `K(X)` by taking germs at `η`. This file exploits
    14	this to present every Čech Picard class (`AlgebraicJacobian.Picard.Pic`) *meromorphically*:
    15	by a pointed cover, a unit cocycle on it, and rational functions `f x ∈ K(X)ˣ`, one per
    16	member, whose ratios `f x / f y` are the germs at `η` of the cocycle values. All cochain
    17	comparisons downstream then happen inside `K(X)ˣ`, where gluing is literal equality of
    18	field elements.
    19	
    20	## Main declarations
    21	
    22	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.germGenericUnits`: the embedding `Γ(X, U)ˣ →* K(X)ˣ` of unit
    23	  sections over an open containing `η` into the units of the function field, with its
    24	  restriction-invariance (`germGenericUnits_unitsRestrict`) and injectivity
    25	  (`germGenericUnits_injective`, on an integral scheme).
    26	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.PointedCover.genericPoint_mem_opens`: on an irreducible
    27	  scheme every member of a pointed cover contains the generic point.
    28	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.MeromorphicPresentation`: the presentation structure — a
    29	  pointed cover, a unit cocycle, and elements `elem x ∈ K(X)ˣ` with
    30	  `elem x / elem y = germ_η (cocycle x y)` — and its Picard class
    31	  `MeromorphicPresentation.picClass`.
    32	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.MeromorphicPresentation.ofCocycle`: the base-index
    33	  construction presenting any unit cocycle: `elem x := germ_η (cocycle x η)`, using the
    34	  generic point itself as the (canonical) base index.
    35	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.exists_meromorphicPresentation`: every Čech Picard class of
    36	  an integral scheme admits a meromorphic presentation (the W1 keystone).
    37	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.LocalEquations.presentation`: the meromorphic presentation of
    38	  a local-equation system — the germs at `η` of its regular equations — with the same
    39	  Picard class (`LocalEquations.presentation_picClass`).
    40	-/
    41	
    42	set_option autoImplicit false
    43	
    44	universe u
    45	
    46	open CategoryTheory Opposite CategoryTheory.PresheafOfGroups
    47	
    48	namespace AlgebraicGeometry
    49	
    50	namespace Scheme
    51	
    52	variable {X : Scheme.{u}} [IsIntegral X]
    53	
    54	/-! ## Unit sections as units of the function field -/
    55	
    56	/-- The embedding of unit sections over an open containing the generic point into the
    57	units of the function field: the germ-at-`η` map on units. -/
    58	noncomputable def germGenericUnits {U : X.Opens} (hηU : genericPoint X ∈ U) :
    59	    Γ(X, U)ˣ →* X.functionFieldˣ :=
    60	  Units.map (X.presheaf.germ U (genericPoint X) hηU).hom
    61	
    62	/-- The underlying rational function of an embedded unit section is the germ at `η` of
    63	its underlying section. -/
    64	@[simp]
    65	lemma germGenericUnits_val {U : X.Opens} (hηU : genericPoint X ∈ U) (u : Γ(X, U)ˣ) :
    66	    (germGenericUnits hηU u : X.functionField)
    67	      = (X.presheaf.germ U (genericPoint X) hηU).hom (u : Γ(X, U)) :=
    68	  rfl
    69	
    70	/-- Embedding a restricted unit section gives the embedding of the original unit
    71	section: germs at `η` are restriction-invariant. -/
    72	lemma germGenericUnits_unitsRestrict {U W : X.Opens} (h : W ≤ U)
    73	    (hηW : genericPoint X ∈ W) (u : Γ(X, U)ˣ) :
    74	    germGenericUnits hηW (X.unitsRestrict h u) = germGenericUnits (h hηW) u := by
    75	  refine Units.ext ?_
    76	  rw [germGenericUnits_val, germGenericUnits_val, Units.coe_map, MonoidHom.coe_coe]
    77	  exact X.presheaf.germ_res_apply (homOfLE h) (genericPoint X) hηW (u : Γ(X, U))
    78	
    79	/-- On an integral scheme the embedding of unit sections into `K(X)ˣ` is injective:
    80	sections are determined by their germs at the generic point. -/
    81	lemma germGenericUnits_injective {U : X.Opens}
    82	    (hηU : genericPoint X ∈ U) :
    83	    Function.Injective (germGenericUnits (X := X) hηU) := by
    84	  intro u v huv
    85	  refine Units.ext (germ_injective_of_isIntegral X (genericPoint X) hηU ?_)
    86	  exact congrArg Units.val huv

    88	/-! ## Pointed covers and the generic point -/
    89	
    90	namespace PointedCover
    91	
    92	variable (𝒰 : X.PointedCover)
    93	
    94	/-- On an irreducible scheme, every member of a pointed cover contains the generic
    95	point: it contains its point, so it is nonempty. -/
    96	lemma genericPoint_mem_opens (x : X) : genericPoint X ∈ 𝒰.opens x :=
    97	  genericPoint_mem_of_nonempty ⟨x, 𝒰.mem_opens x⟩
    98	
    99	/-- On an irreducible scheme, every pairwise overlap of a pointed cover contains the
   100	generic point. -/
   101	lemma genericPoint_mem_inf (x y : X) : genericPoint X ∈ 𝒰.opens x ⊓ 𝒰.opens y :=
   102	  ⟨𝒰.genericPoint_mem_opens x, 𝒰.genericPoint_mem_opens y⟩
   103	
   104	end PointedCover
   105	
   106	omit [IsIntegral X] in
   107	/-- Restriction of a unit Čech `H¹` class along a refinement, on a cocycle
   108	representative: the class of the restricted cocycle. -/
   109	lemma unitsRes_class {𝒰 𝒲 : X.PointedCover} (h : 𝒲 ≤ 𝒰) (γ : X.unitsCocycle 𝒰) :
   110	    unitsRes h γ.class = (γ.res fun x ↦ homOfLE (h x)).class :=
   111	  rfl
   112	
   113	/-! ## Meromorphic presentations -/
   114	
   115	/-- A **meromorphic presentation** of a Čech Picard class on an integral scheme: a
   116	pointed cover, a unit cocycle on it, and rational functions `elem x ∈ K(X)ˣ`, one per
   117	member, whose ratios are the germs at `η` of the cocycle values:
   118	`elem x / elem y = germ_η (cocycle x y)`.
   119	
   120	The elements `elem` are a meromorphic trivialization of the class `picClass` of the
   121	cocycle; their zero/pole orders cut out its divisor
   122	(`AlgebraicJacobian.Picard.PresentationDivisor`). -/
   123	structure MeromorphicPresentation (X : Scheme.{u}) [IsIntegral X] : Type u where
   124	  /-- The pointed cover carrying the presented cocycle. -/
   125	  cover : X.PointedCover
   126	  /-- The presented unit Čech 1-cocycle. -/
   127	  cocycle : X.unitsCocycle cover
   128	  /-- The meromorphic trivialization: one unit of the function field per member. -/
   129	  elem : X → X.functionFieldˣ
   130	  /-- The ratio property: on each pair, the ratio of the trivializing elements is the
   131	  germ at `η` of the cocycle value. -/
   132	  ratio : ∀ x y : X, elem x * (elem y)⁻¹
   133	    = germGenericUnits (cover.genericPoint_mem_inf x y) (unitsEvInf cocycle x y)
   134	
   135	namespace MeromorphicPresentation
   136	
   137	/-- The Čech Picard class presented by a meromorphic presentation. -/
   138	def picClass (P : X.MeromorphicPresentation) : X.CechPic :=
   139	  CechPic.mk P.cover P.cocycle.class
   140	
   141	/-- The base-index construction: any unit cocycle `γ` on a pointed cover is presented
   142	meromorphically by `elem x := germ_η (γ x η)`, taking the generic point itself as the
   143	canonical base index (all overlaps contain `η`, so the cocycle identity for the triple
   144	`(x, y, η)` becomes the ratio property in `K(X)ˣ`). -/
   145	noncomputable def ofCocycle (𝒰 : X.PointedCover) (γ : X.unitsCocycle 𝒰) :
   146	    X.MeromorphicPresentation where
   147	  cover := 𝒰
   148	  cocycle := γ
   149	  elem x := germGenericUnits (𝒰.genericPoint_mem_inf x (genericPoint X))
   150	    (unitsEvInf γ x (genericPoint X))
   151	  ratio x y := by
   152	    have hηT : genericPoint X
   153	        ∈ 𝒰.opens x ⊓ 𝒰.opens y ⊓ 𝒰.opens (genericPoint X) :=
   154	      ⟨𝒰.genericPoint_mem_inf x y, 𝒰.genericPoint_mem_opens (genericPoint X)⟩
   155	    have key := congrArg (germGenericUnits hηT)
   156	      (unitsEvInf_trans γ x y (genericPoint X))
   157	    rw [map_mul, germGenericUnits_unitsRestrict, germGenericUnits_unitsRestrict,
   158	      germGenericUnits_unitsRestrict] at key
   159	    rw [mul_inv_eq_iff_eq_mul]
   160	    exact key.symm
   161	
   162	@[simp]
   163	lemma ofCocycle_picClass (𝒰 : X.PointedCover) (γ : X.unitsCocycle 𝒰) :
   164	    (ofCocycle 𝒰 γ).picClass = CechPic.mk 𝒰 γ.class :=
   165	  rfl
   166	
   167	end MeromorphicPresentation
   168	
   169	/-- **Existence of meromorphic presentations** (the W1 keystone): every Čech Picard
   170	class of an integral scheme is the class of a meromorphic presentation. -/
   171	theorem exists_meromorphicPresentation (L : X.CechPic) :
   172	    ∃ P : X.MeromorphicPresentation, P.picClass = L := by
   173	  induction L using CechPic.ind with | _ 𝒰 a =>
   174	  induction a using Quot.ind with | _ γ =>
   175	  exact ⟨MeromorphicPresentation.ofCocycle 𝒰 γ, rfl⟩
   176	
   177	/-! ## The presentation of a local-equation system -/
   178	
   179	namespace LocalEquations
   180	
   181	variable (E : X.LocalEquations)
   182	
   183	/-- The germ at `η` of a local equation is a nonzero rational function: the equation is
   184	regular, so its germ at the generic point is a nonzerodivisor of the field `K(X)`. -/
   185	lemma germGeneric_eqn_ne_zero (x : X) :
   186	    (X.presheaf.germ (E.cover.opens x) (genericPoint X)
   187	        (E.cover.genericPoint_mem_opens x)).hom (E.eqn x) ≠ (0 : X.functionField) := by
   188	  have h : (X.presheaf.germ (E.cover.opens x) (genericPoint X)
   189	        (E.cover.genericPoint_mem_opens x)).hom (E.eqn x)
   190	      ∈ nonZeroDivisors X.functionField :=
   191	    E.regular x (genericPoint X) (E.cover.genericPoint_mem_opens x)
   192	  exact mem_nonZeroDivisors_iff_ne_zero.mp h
   193	
   194	/-- The meromorphic presentation of a local-equation system: the trivializing elements
   195	are the germs at `η` of the regular equations, and the presented cocycle is the cocycle
   196	of transition units. The ratio property is the defining equation `eqn x = g x y · eqn y`
   197	pushed to the generic point. -/
   198	noncomputable def presentation : X.MeromorphicPresentation where
   199	  cover := E.cover
   200	  cocycle := E.unitsCocycle
   201	  elem x := Units.mk0 _ (E.germGeneric_eqn_ne_zero x)
   202	  ratio x y := by
   203	    refine Units.ext ?_
   204	    have key := congrArg
   205	      (X.presheaf.germ (E.cover.opens x ⊓ E.cover.opens y) (genericPoint X)
   206	        (E.cover.genericPoint_mem_inf x y)).hom (E.eqn_restrict_eq x y)
   207	    rw [map_mul, X.presheaf.germ_res_apply, X.presheaf.germ_res_apply] at key
   208	    rw [Units.val_mul, Units.val_inv_eq_inv_val, Units.val_mk0, Units.val_mk0,
   209	      unitsCocycle_evInf, germGenericUnits_val,
   210	      mul_inv_eq_iff_eq_mul₀ (E.germGeneric_eqn_ne_zero y)]
   211	    exact key
   212	
   213	/-- The presentation of a local-equation system presents its Picard class. -/
   214	@[simp]
   215	lemma presentation_picClass : E.presentation.picClass = E.picClass :=
   216	  rfl
   217	
   218	@[simp]
   219	lemma presentation_cover : E.presentation.cover = E.cover :=
   220	  rfl
   221	
   222	@[simp]
   223	lemma presentation_cocycle : E.presentation.cocycle = E.unitsCocycle :=
   224	  rfl
   225	
   226	/-- The trivializing element of the presentation of a local-equation system is the germ
   227	at `η` of its equation. -/
   228	lemma presentation_elem_val (x : X) :
   229	    (E.presentation.elem x : X.functionField)
   230	      = (X.presheaf.germ (E.cover.opens x) (genericPoint X)
   231	          (E.cover.genericPoint_mem_opens x)).hom (E.eqn x) :=
   232	  rfl
   233	
   234	end LocalEquations
   235	
   236	end Scheme

   238	end AlgebraicGeometry

    10	/-!
    11	# W6-full: the glued sheaf of a meromorphic presentation is the divisor sheaf (DAT-3 (c))
    12	
    13	For the curve bundle `X` — integral, smooth of relative dimension one and quasi-compact
    14	over a field `K` — and a meromorphic presentation `P` (`Scheme.MeromorphicPresentation`:
    15	a pointed cover, a unit cocycle on it, and trivializing elements `P.elem x ∈ K(X)ˣ` whose
    16	ratios are the germs at `η` of the cocycle values), this file identifies the m-chart
    17	cocycle-glued sheaf of `P` with the divisor sheaf of its presentation divisor — the core
    18	of the W6-full seam (`informal/w4-datum-worksheet.md` §3.1(c), spec FROZEN there):
    19	
    20	* `Scheme.MeromorphicPresentation.isGluingCocycle` — the presentation's cocycle satisfies
    21	  the gluing cocycle law (`unit_self` from the ratio property at `(x, x)` through the
    22	  injective germ embedding; `mul_res` is the landed `unitsEvInf_trans`);
    23	* `Scheme.MeromorphicPresentation.gluedSheaf` — the glued sheaf of `K`-modules of the
    24	  presentation, `AlgebraicGeometry.gluedSheaf` on `P.cover.opens` with multipliers the
    25	  pair values of `P.cocycle`;
    26	* `Scheme.MeromorphicPresentation.gluedDivisorSheafIso` —
    27	  **`glued(P) ≅ 𝒪(presentationDivisor P)`**: over a nonempty open the components send a
    28	  matching family `s` to the rational function `(P.elem x)⁻¹ · germ_η (s x)` (independent
    29	  of the piece `x` — `gluedVal_eq_elem_inv_mul`); the inverse trivializes a bounded
    30	  rational function `h` chartwise as the section with germ `P.elem x · h` (the
    31	  `mulEquivDivisorSheaf` mechanism, chartwise, through the `𝒪(0) ≅ 𝒪_X` gluing engine
    32	  `exists_section_germ_eq`).
    33	
    34	## The pole-bound bridge
    35	
    36	At a closed point `z` of a piece, the divisor bound of `presentationDivisor K P` is the
    37	coerced order `ordZ_z (P.elem z)` (`divisorBound_presentationDivisor`), and every piece
    38	element `P.elem x` with `z` in its piece has the same order (`ordZ_elem_eq`). So
    39	multiplication by `P.elem x` converts the pole bound `D` into the pole bound `0` exactly,
    40	and integrality glues to honest sections by the landed `𝒪(0) ≅ 𝒪_X` machinery.
    41	
    42	The `Subsingleton`/`h⁰`/FLV consequences (the `hfib` sheaf-form discharge and the rank
    43	export) are assembled in `AlgebraicJacobian.RiemannRoch.W6Full`.
    44	-/
